name: What are SSH Keys?
description:
Introduction to SSH Keys

SSH keys provide a more secure way to log into a server than using passwords. A key pair consists of:

  • Private key — stays on your machine (never share this!)
  • Public key — placed on servers you want to access

When you connect, the server checks if your private key matches the public key. No password needed.

Check if you already have SSH keys:

$ ls -la ~/.ssh/

If you see id_rsa and id_rsa.pub, you already have a key pair. If the directory doesn't exist or is empty, we'll create one in the next step.
answer: SSH keys are much more secure than passwords because they can't be brute-forced and are typically 2048+ bits long.

name: Generating a Key Pair
description:
Creating SSH Keys

Generate a new RSA key pair:

$ ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096

You'll be prompted for:

Enter file in which to save the key (/root/.ssh/id_rsa): [Press Enter]
Enter passphrase: [Press Enter for no passphrase]
Enter same passphrase again: [Press Enter]

This creates two files:

$ ls ~/.ssh/
id_rsa      ← private key (KEEP SECRET)
id_rsa.pub  ← public key (share this)

View your public key:

$ cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub

You'll see a long string starting with ssh-rsa AAAA...

name: Key File Permissions
description:
Correct Permissions

SSH is strict about file permissions. If they're wrong, SSH will refuse to use your keys.

The correct permissions are:

$ chmod 700 ~/.ssh
$ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa
$ chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
$ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Check them:

$ ls -la ~/.ssh/

You should see:

drwx------  .ssh/
-rw-------  id_rsa
-rw-r--r--  id_rsa.pub
-rw-------  authorized_keys

If the private key has wrong permissions (e.g., readable by others), SSH will show:

WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!
answer: The private key (id_rsa) must be readable only by the owner — chmod 600. This is a common interview question!

name: Setting Up Passwordless Login
description:
Copying Your Public Key

To enable key-based login to a server, you need to put your public key in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file.

For this tutorial, let's set it up for localhost (same machine).

The easy way — using ssh-copy-id:

$ ssh-copy-id root@localhost

Enter the password when prompted. It copies your public key automatically.

The manual way:

$ cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Now test it — you should NOT be asked for a password:

$ ssh root@localhost whoami

If it prints root without asking for a password, key authentication is working!

name: SSH Config File
description:
Simplifying SSH Connections

Instead of typing long SSH commands, create a config file:

$ vim ~/.ssh/config

Add entries like this:

Host myserver
    HostName 192.168.1.100
    User admin
    Port 22
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa

Host webserver
    HostName 10.0.0.50
    User deploy
    Port 2222

Now instead of:

$ ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa -p 2222 deploy@10.0.0.50

You just type:

$ ssh webserver

Set correct permissions on the config file:

$ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config

name: Different Key Types
description:
Key Algorithms

RSA isn't the only option. Modern alternatives:

Ed25519 — recommended, faster, shorter keys:

$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519

ECDSA — elliptic curve:

$ ssh-keygen -t ecdsa -b 521

Compare key sizes:

$ cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub | wc -c      # RSA: ~750 characters
$ cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | wc -c   # Ed25519: ~100 characters

Ed25519 is just as secure but much shorter. Many sysadmins are switching to it.

You can have multiple key pairs and specify which one to use in ~/.ssh/config.
answer: Ed25519 is the recommended algorithm for new keys. RSA 4096-bit is still fine but Ed25519 is faster and more modern.

name: Disabling Password Login
description:
Hardening SSH

Once key authentication works, you can disable password login entirely.

Edit the SSH server config:

$ vim /etc/ssh/sshd_config

Find and change these lines:

PasswordAuthentication no
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no

Also ensure key authentication is enabled:

PubkeyAuthentication yes

Restart SSH to apply:

$ systemctl restart sshd

Warning: Make sure your key login works BEFORE disabling passwords! Otherwise you'll lock yourself out.

Test in a new terminal before closing your current session:

$ ssh root@localhost
answer: Always test key-based login in a separate session before disabling password authentication. This is the #1 way admins lock themselves out.
